newsitem.title: USA: Dalmatians memorabilia have heyday with new movie.
newsitem.headline: Dalmatians memorabilia have heyday with new movie.

text.p: Disney dogs are having their day as the new "101 Dalmatians" live-action movie sends collectors on a chase for memorabilia related to the original cartoon.
It's rough if you want a videotape of the 1961 classic to show your kids. The tapes, which were issued in 1983 at $18 apiece, now sell for up to $200 at dealerships -- if you can find them.

"I'm getting more calls than ever about the '101 Dalmatians' videotape not sold in stores," said Joel Cohen of Cohen Books & Collectibles in Boca Raton, Fla. (407 487-7888), which specialises in vintage Disney memorabilia. "It was much cheaper, by at least $100, before the new movie came out."
Don't call Cohen. He doesn't have any left.
If you want a piece of the animation action on your wall, expect to pay about 30 percent more for the original artwork than just a few weeks ago.
Christie's and Sotheby's are riding the doggie bandwagon by holding their twice-annual animation art auctions this week, starring villainess Cruella DeVil and the Dalmatians.

The most popular items among collectors are vintage cels, the handpainted transparencies used to make cartoon films until the 1970s. Cartoons are now made with computer-generated pictures, which have no value as original art.
A cel showing an angry Cruella talking on a demon-shaped phone from her bed while clutching her pink cigarette in a blue holder is expected to fetch $4,000 to $6,000 at Sotheby's on Saturday.
A cel from the film which features the canine sweethearts, Pongo and Perdita, is estimated to raise $7,000 to $9,000.
At Christie's auction Thursday, two cels of the Dalmatian pups' parents, are expected to sell for $4,000 to $6,000 each.

"My guess is that Dalmatian (cel) prices have increased 20 percent to 30 percent" because of the new movie, said Elyse Luray-Marx, assistant vice president at Christie's East. "It's strictly a guess."

Not bad for pieces of celluloid that you could buy at Disneyland in the 1960s for about $5 each. Prices of 1930s Disneyana were doubling every six months in the late 1980s, dealers said. Items signed by Walt Disney now average about $1,000 apiece, up from $500 to $700 in 1990.

But don't assume that prices will just keep going up. Animation art had its dog days in 1991 and 1992 after soaring in the 1980s, when cash-rich collectors snapped up what they thought were once-in-a-lifetime bargains. The market for Disney toys, especially 1930s tin wind-ups, has also slumped in recent years. All because more than a few cels and other memorabilia emerged from attics and basements, and some key collectors dropped out.

A six-inch 1930s porcelain figure of Donald Duck with movable arms that a dealer bought for $2,500 around 1990 could find no buyers at $600 two years later, said Paul Anderson, a dealer and publisher of a magazine on Disney's history and Disneyana (801 967-3955).
With new memorabilia, such as "101 Dalmatians" souvenirs, Disney fans tend to get caught up in the hype of the moment and often make impulsive purchases, pushing up prices briefly.

"Vintage collectibles will shoot up 30 percent to 50 percent" as a result of the movie, which topped the box-office chart in the past two weeks, Anderson said. "The new stuff will double (in price) and settle back to where it was in six to eight months."
It's history repeating itself.
For example, a complete set of 40 trading cards commemorating Disneyland's 40th anniversary in 1995 were worth $650 then, but sell for only $100 now.
When Euro Disney opened outside Paris in 1992, collectors who had not been there spent $25 to $40 for a map of the theme park. You can pick one up now for $6 to $8.
So, continue to paws -- er, pause -- and snap up Dalmatian bargains down the road.

"If you're looking for an investment, be extremely cautious," Anderson said. "Be wary. It's easy to get caught up in Disney's marketing frenzy and pay too much. If you really want it, wait two to three months and you can find it for considerably less."
